name: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis
lead: Mandibular distraction osteogenesis (MDO) is a surgical technique that lengthens the lower jaw gradually. The bone is cut and the segments are slowly separated by a device, so new bone forms in the gap.[7][8] The principle derives from Ilizarov's work on long bones, who showed bone forms when stretched along its axis at about 1 mm per day.[3]

The modern clinical era in the jaw is dated to 1992 reports of gradual mandibular lengthening by McCarthy and colleagues.[7] A 1995 report described an oblique corticotomy technique used in 87 patients.[1] Its best-documented uses are in mandibular hypoplasia such as hemifacial microsomia and Treacher Collins syndrome, and in infants with micrognathia and airway obstruction, such as in Pierre Robin sequence.[2][6][9][10]

Published evidence is mostly case series and cohort reports in children with congenital conditions. In looksmaxxing culture it is mentioned among procedures for adults seeking mandibular advancement; no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity have been published.

paras: The idea of lengthening bone by gradual separation was first proposed by Bernhard von Langenbeck in 1869, according to Wikipedia, and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, lengthening femurs in 26 people born with malformed legs; complications such as infection and nonunion were high and the method was not adopted.[7] Wolfgang Rosenthal is credited with the first use in the jaw in 1930, but jaw use was not explored further until the 1980s.[7]

The method became widespread through Gavriil Ilizarov (1921-1992), a Soviet orthopaedic surgeon who in 1951 built an external frame after finding that a carefully cut bone with its surrounding membrane intact could be gradually separated and would regrow to fill the gap.[17] He became head of trauma and orthopaedics at a regional hospital in Kurgan in 1955 and founded a research institute there in 1971.[17] Moscow's medical establishment initially resisted him; the treatment of Olympic high jumper Valeriy Brumel in 1968 raised his profile, and the Italian mountaineer Carlo Mauri's 1980 treatment in Kurgan led to Ilizarov's first lecture outside the Soviet bloc, in Bellagio in 1981.[17] Wikipedia says Ilizarov studied distraction in more than 15,000 people.[7]

The first modern clinical report of gradual mandibular lengthening came from McCarthy and colleagues in 1992.[7] Since the 1980s the jaw applications have centred on hemifacial microsomia, micrognathia, craniofrontonasal dysplasia and craniosynostosis, plus airway obstruction in infants.[7]

The phases are osteotomy with device placement, a latency of about a week, activation at roughly 1 mm per day, and consolidation before the device is removed in a second operation.[7] Devices can be external frames, which allow monitoring but carry pin-site infection and scarring risk, or buried intraoral distractors, which reduce those risks but demand accurate planning.[8] One summary gives mandibular advancements of about 10-24 mm.[8]

Biological work in animals has shown that blood vessel formation and the mechanical environment are required for bone induction during distraction.[4] A 2018 mouse study reported that mechanoresponsive stem cells acquire neural crest fate in jaw regeneration.[5]

Separation that is too fast risks nonunion, in which fibrous tissue forms instead of bone, while separation that is too slow risks premature union.[7] Wikipedia also notes devices using springs for continuous tension instead of manual steps.[7]

Studies have examined distraction to relieve upper airway obstruction in young children with craniofacial deformities,[2][10] including in neonates as a strategy to avoid tracheostomy[9] and as part of an algorithm for isolated Pierre Robin sequence.[11] A 2001 study of ten patients aged 3 months to 8 years measured airway cross-sectional area changes.[2] Reviews of infant sleep apnea discuss obstructive causes.[12]

A 2001 review of 3,278 craniofacial distraction cases is a major source on complications.[13] Wikipedia summarizes figures of about 5% infection, 7-9% bone growing in an unintended direction, 3-4.5% hardware failure, and in mandibular distraction about 3.5% inferior alveolar nerve damage, 2% tooth bud injury and 0.5% facial nerve injury.[7] Another summary reports pin-site infection in roughly 6-27% of sites and reports that complication rates fall with surgeon experience.[8]
The Wikipedia summary also lists protocol failure at about 4.5% and pain ending the procedure at about 1%.[7]

Within looksmaxxing communities, mandibular distraction is mentioned among procedures for adults seeking mandibular advancement, a longer or more forward lower jaw. It is a staged surgical route in which a device stays in place for weeks while the bone lengthens, in contrast with single-stage jaw surgery.

Published surgical literature describes the procedure mainly for congenital jaw deficiency and airway obstruction rather than for cosmetic enhancement of a normal jaw, and a 2016 systematic review summarised on Wikipedia found the mandibular studies too low in quality and too varied to combine, with significant vertical relapse.[7]

Human evidence includes the 87-patient 1995 series,[1] the 2001 ten-patient airway study,[2] and the 3,278-case review.[13] Registered studies include computer-guided distraction in hemifacial microsomia (n=12),[14] CAD/CAM surgical templates for mandible distraction (n=30),[15] and a comparison of internal and external distractors (n=30).[16]

Randomised trials have compared distraction with sagittal split ramus osteotomy (SSRO): one trial compared the two procedures in mandibular advancement,[18] another compared skeletal stability after each,[20] and trials in obstructive sleep apnea compared them for airway outcomes, with an 18-patient randomised study following quality of life after skeletal advancement by SSRO or distraction.[19][21] A review of Treacher Collins mandibular distraction describes the technique as a way to correct the steep occlusal plane and mandibular deficiency typical of that syndrome and reports that it can greatly improve quality of life.[22]

A 2016 systematic review summarised on Wikipedia found the mandibular studies too heterogeneous for meta-analysis, noted significant vertical relapse that was higher with a high initial gonial angle, and reported about 90% sagittal soft-tissue correspondence to the bone movement.[7] An animal study in rabbits reported that the distracted mandible did not reach the same strength as a normal mandible.[23] No studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.

card.summary: Gradual lower-jaw lengthening with a bone-stretching device, well documented in children with congenital conditions, unstudied for purely cosmetic use.
card.note: Evidence is from congenital and airway cases; nerve injury and infection are documented complications.

quick.overview:
Mandibular distraction cuts the lower jaw and slowly stretches the gap with a device so new bone forms. It is established for children with small jaws and airway obstruction, such as Pierre Robin sequence.

The literature is mainly case series and cohort reports; no studies of cosmetic use in people without a deformity were found.
quick.mechanism: After a cut and a week-long latency, the device lengthens the jaw at about 1 mm per day, followed by a consolidation period as bone matures. Devices can be external or internal.
quick.risks: A large review of 3,278 craniofacial cases documents complications; summaries report infection, hardware failure, and inferior alveolar nerve, tooth bud or facial nerve injury in a minority of cases.

angle.goal: Jaw size and profile (chin and lower-face projection)
chain: Bone is cut and the jaw segments are separated about 1 mm a day
New bone forms in the gap, advancing the lower jaw
A longer, more forward mandible changes chin projection and facial profile
angle.text: Distraction lengthens the lower jaw with the patient's own new bone, which can move the chin and jaw forward further than a single-stage cut allows. In clinical practice it is used for small or underdeveloped jaws, and in looksmaxxing discussion it is mentioned as a route to a larger, more projected lower face.
